evaluation.positioning_hook: A self-doubting teen in a small Midwest town discovers she’s a shapeshifting test subject, then has to outwit a biotech cover-up before the company turns her into its billionaire puppet.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is immediately legible and commercially sticky: a teen discovers she can copy anyone she touches while a corporate security team hunts her through school, mall, and woods. The audience lane is real and broad enough for genre buyers, though the body-swap mechanics and conspiracy density keep it from feeling four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands fast in the opening chase and gets sharpened by the roadside reveal, the school confrontation, and the later identity twist. By the time Ava changes into Christy and then learns she may actually be Madison, the premise is clear and escalating.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ava/Madison is a strong lead because she’s insecure, morally stubborn, and physically transformative in a way that externalizes her self-image. June, Shannon, Priscilla, and David all have distinct energy, but the script is still most durable around the lead rather than a deep bench.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar chase/conspiracy setup and makes the central mechanic emotional rather than just tactical: identity is literally transferable, unstable, and contagious. The Ava/Madison reveal and the final choice to preserve selfhood give the material a bolder conceptual spine than a standard escape thriller.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps turning the screw: roadside chase, school extraction, mall escape, mansion reveal, lab siege, and final shutdown. Each sequence changes the rules or the stakes, and the ending earns its forward motion rather than coasting.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a girl who can become anyone she touches, only to discover she’s been living inside someone else’s identity, is both strange and instantly playable. It feels fresh because the emotional question and the genre engine are the same thing.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The small-town corporate occupation, school intrusion, mall camouflage, and secret-lab hierarchy create a usable world with social pressure and procedural texture. It’s not a sprawling mythology piece, but the setting keeps generating story through security protocols, disinformation, and class tension.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct register: teen awkwardness, body-horror panic, and deadpan social comedy all live in the same frame. The burger-joint crush scene, the mall disguise sequence, and the final found-family release give it a tone that’s hard to mistake for anything else.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the chase mechanics, the script is about class resentment, maternal sacrifice, self-loathing, and the seduction of power. The Ava/Madison identity fracture and David’s attachment to her suggest more emotional depth than the surface thriller initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ava and June have a strong mother-daughter engine, Shannon gives the teen world a lived-in counterpoint, and David/Priscilla/Wolcott create a functional antagonist system. The relationships are active enough to keep scenes generating, even though the script is still fundamentally lead-driven.

lead_characters.name: Ava
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16, high-school age, working-class suburban teen; later revealed to be Madison in Ava’s body/form.
lead_characters.hook: Ava presents as a sharp, self-conscious teen who thinks she’s plain, small, and stuck in a life that doesn’t fit her. She’s funny, observant, and morally stubborn, but the script’s real engine is that her identity is unstable in the deepest possible way: she can become whoever she touches, and she may not actually be Ava at all. That contradiction gives the role a constant push-pull between vulnerability, physical power, and existential panic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is showcase territory in the vein of Saoirse Ronan in 'Lady Bird' colliding with the body-switch volatility of Toni Collette in 'Hereditary'—a role that asks for comedy, fear, rage, and identity collapse in the same performance. It gives an actor a rare chance to play emotional truth while physically inhabiting multiple forms.

lead_characters.name: June
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-30s, blue-collar mother, working-class, tattooed, hard-edged but loving.
lead_characters.hook: June is a scrappy, overextended single mom whose humor masks real exhaustion and survival instinct. She starts as the kind of parent who seems chaotic and under-resourced, then reveals she can move from defensive sarcasm to ferocious protectiveness instantly. Her own shapeshifting turns her into a surprising mirror of her daughter: a woman who has spent years changing shape just to keep the family afloat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Allison Janney in 'I, Tonya' and Patricia Clarkson in 'Sharp Objects' their bite—sharp comic timing, bruised authority, and a late-arriving emotional ferocity. It’s a mother role with teeth, not wallpaper.

lead_characters.name: Shannon
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16, high-school age, Ava’s best friend, full-figured, curly-haired, socially grounded.
lead_characters.hook: Shannon is the best-friend role that keeps the movie human: funny, loyal, practical, and often the first person to call out Ava’s self-absorption. She gives the script a normal-teen baseline, but she’s also smart enough to track the conspiracy before most adults do. She’s the kind of supporting part that can steal scenes without ever hijacking the story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, scene-stealing teen-friend role that made Auli’i Cravalho in 'The Little Mermaid' and Beanie Feldstein in 'Booksmart' feel instantly watchable. It offers comic rhythm, emotional loyalty, and a real friendship dynamic.

lead_characters.name: Priscilla
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 40s, corporate security lead, authoritative, polished, intimidating.
lead_characters.hook: Priscilla is the face of the operation: controlled, smart, and capable of sounding reasonable while doing monstrous things. She’s not a cackling villain; she’s a professional who believes she’s managing a crisis, which makes her more dangerous. The role has a great mix of command, menace, and bureaucratic self-justification.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of authority role that gave Viola Davis in 'Widows' and Carrie Coon in 'The Leftovers' such command—an actor gets to play intelligence, pressure, and moral compromise without losing control of the room. It’s a premium antagonist part.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.demographics: Male, elderly, shapeshifter trapped in multiple bodies; identity fluid, emotionally damaged, cognitively fractured.
lead_characters.hook: David is the script’s most tragic wild card: a man whose body and self have been broken apart by the experiment, leaving him desperate for connection and increasingly unstable. He can be tender, manipulative, frightened, and dangerous in the same scene. The role becomes especially potent because his bond with Madison is both protective and deeply compromised.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of transformation-heavy, psychologically layered part that gave Gary Oldman in 'Darkest Hour' and Paul Dano in 'The Batman' their showcase value—an actor gets to disappear into physicality while carrying real emotional damage. It’s a performance role with major range.

lead_characters.name: Wolcott
lead_characters.hook: Wolcott is the intellectual horror of the piece: a man who can talk about curing cancer and reversing aging while overseeing torture. He’s not flashy, but he’s chilling because he believes his own logic. He gives the movie its most overtly predatory corporate-science energy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of icy authority role that lets an actor do what Michael Keaton did in 'Dopesick' or Bryan Cranston did in 'Your Honor'—project intelligence, entitlement, and menace with minimal movement. It’s a prestige villain part.

lead_characters.name: Jamieson
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-40s, private-security enforcer, physically imposing, tactical.
lead_characters.hook: Jamieson is the blunt instrument of the operation: the guy who keeps the chase moving, applies force, and turns every scene into a threat assessment. He’s less psychologically complex than Priscilla or Wolcott, but he’s useful because he makes the danger feel immediate and physical.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid heavy territory in the lane of Shea Whigham or Michael Shannon—an actor gets to play controlled aggression and tactical menace without needing speeches. It’s a strong utility antagonist role.

lead_characters.name: Mills
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, ex-military/private security, conflicted, physically capable.
lead_characters.hook: Mills is the most human of the company enforcers, which makes him useful and dangerous at once. He’s clearly complicit, but the script gives him enough guilt and fatigue to suggest a conscience under the uniform. That makes him a credible pivot point when the story needs a crack in the machine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of conflicted enforcer role that gives actors like Boyd Holbrook or Ben Foster a lot to play—physical competence, moral corrosion, and the possibility of a turn. It’s a good showcase for controlled intensity.

lead_characters.name: Wilma
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, company nurse/handler, observant, professional, deceptively warm.
lead_characters.hook: Wilma is the soft-spoken face of coercion: she can sound caring while participating in a system that strips people of agency. She’s especially effective because she’s the one who explains the rules, then becomes one of the story’s casualties. The role gives the movie a human-scale betrayal inside the larger conspiracy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Jodie Comer did in 'Killing Eve' or Merritt Wever does in prestige drama—calm surface, hidden threat, and emotional ambiguity. It’s a deceptively rich supporting part.

lead_characters.name: Eric Huntington
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 50s, billionaire tech mogul, vain, charismatic, predatory.
lead_characters.hook: Eric is the absent center of the conspiracy: a rich, self-regarding power broker whose body becomes the prize everyone is fighting over. He’s not on the page for long, but he matters because the entire operation is built around his money, his image, and his appetite. The role functions as the story’s ultimate mask of power.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a juicy, limited but memorable role in the lane of Jeremy Strong in 'The Big Short' or Armie Hammer in 'The Social Network'—a character who embodies wealth, entitlement, and institutional rot. It’s a prestige-cameo part with real narrative weight.

casting_characteristics: one child lead with extensive emotional and physical transformation
adult actors required to play multiple identities/forms

notable_requirements: small-town woods and roadside chase corridor
high school interiors and exterior parking lot
mall concourse, bathrooms, and dressing rooms
secret lab / warehouse / morgue set build
suburban ranch house and townhouse safe house

technical.vfx_details: Frequent shapeshift transformations, body-morphing effects, foam reactions, fire ignition, and a few stylized chase beats; most of the movie is practical, but the identity-change moments need strong digital augmentation.
technical.sfx_needs: Cattle prods, gunfire, vehicle chase beats, falls, restraint work, fire/sprinkler sequence, and practical foam effects.

rights_flags.detail: Eric Huntington is a fictional character, but the script references the New York Times, CNN, and a billionaire tech mogul archetype without naming a real person.
TikTok, Trader Joe’s, iPhone, Ford Escape, Honda Civic, Mercedes SUV, Beretta APX Carry, and Purina are all named or clearly branded in the script.
Indiana Jones is referenced by title in dialogue.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: streamer original or specialty theatrical with genre marketing and strong trailer hook.

budget.note: Contemporary setting keeps the spend contained, but the shapeshift effects, multiple identity changes, school/mall/woods coverage, and the secret-lab fire sequence push this above a simple contained thriller.

casting.note: The lead has to play a teen girl, a child, multiple adult bodies, and the emotional continuity across all of them; that is a narrow and unusually demanding casting lift.

development.note: The identity reveal and the Ava/Madison switch are the script’s biggest structural swing, and the movie depends on the audience tracking that logic cleanly while still feeling the emotional loss.

comp_set.title: Freaky
comp_set.why_it_comps: Body-swap mechanics drive both the comedy and the danger, with the lead forced to navigate a new form while being hunted.

comp_set.title: The Faculty
comp_set.why_it_comps: Small-town teen paranoia, covert invasion, and a school setting that becomes the front line of a larger conspiracy.

comp_set.title: Upgrade
comp_set.why_it_comps: A propulsive genre engine built around bodily takeover, escalating violence, and a protagonist whose identity is under siege.

comp_set.title: The Invisible Man
comp_set.why_it_comps: A contemporary thriller that turns a personal violation into a high-concept chase and keeps the audience inside the protagonist’s panic.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre-forward adults and older teens who want a smart, propulsive sci-fi thriller with emotional stakes and a strong female lead.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 16-44, with a slight female lean; strongest with streaming genre audiences, teen/young adult viewers, and adults who like elevated high-concept thrillers.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations keep the budget in indie range, but the transformation effects, action coverage, and secret-lab climax prevent this from being micro.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals dev execs building genre slates
specialty theatrical buyers looking for a high-concept hook
indie producers with VFX-light but concept-forward genre mandates
lane_fit.detail: This sits cleanly in the elevated-genre lane: a female-led, concept-first thriller with emotional stakes, a clear trailer hook, and enough practical production control to feel financeable. The script is strongest for buyers who want a smart hook without tentpole spend.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is intriguing, but the supporting characters do not present a clean spinoff vector beyond this story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The identity hook is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the movie a trailer-ready premise that can be explained fast and remembered even faster. It’s the kind of hook that can sell a buyer on concept before they’ve even met the full mythology, which is exactly what genre financiers want.
strengths.evidence: The opening chase, the roadside shapeshift reveal, and the later discovery that Ava is actually Madison all reframe the same engine in escalating ways.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The lead role is a performance showcase.
strengths.what_it_means: Ava/Madison is not just a plot function; she’s a role that can launch or reframe an actor because the body changes are tied to emotional state. That makes the project attractive to talent reps looking for a part with range, transformation, and awards-adjacent texture inside a commercial package.
strengths.evidence: Ava becomes Christy, Grandma, Eric, and multiple other bodies while the script keeps the emotional throughline intact.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The movie has a clean, marketable lane.
strengths.what_it_means: This is a genre feature that can be sold on premise, tone, and a contained production footprint rather than on expensive IP or star dependency. That makes it especially attractive to streamer genre buyers and indie financiers looking for a controlled upside play.
strengths.evidence: Most of the action lives in contemporary locations—woods, school, mall, house, warehouse, lab—with only moderate VFX and no period burden.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The mother-daughter dynamic adds emotional ballast.
strengths.what_it_means: The script isn’t just about escaping a conspiracy; it’s about a daughter and mother learning how to protect each other when the world has made them both unstable. That widens the appeal beyond pure sci-fi mechanics and gives the ending a genuine emotional payoff.
strengths.evidence: June’s late reveal that she can shapeshift too, and the final found-family alignment with Madison and Real Ava, give the movie heart.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone can pivot without losing the movie.
strengths.what_it_means: The script can move from teen comedy to body horror to corporate thriller without feeling like a different project, which is a real commercial asset. Buyers like material that can play in multiple marketing registers while still feeling coherent.
strengths.evidence: The burger-joint crush scene, the mall disguise sequence, and the lab fire finale all feel like the same movie.

whats_special.headline: This is a high-concept, female-led sci-fi thriller with a rare kind of hook: the body-swap mechanic is also the emotional wound. It’s commercially legible, production-manageable, and built around a lead role that could attract serious talent while still playing cleanly in the genre marketplace.

items.area: The identity reveal is the biggest buyer-risk swing.
items.detail: The Ava/Madison reversal is the movie’s smartest move, but it also asks the audience to reorient its emotional investment midstream. That’s a strong creative choice, but it’s the one place where a producer will worry about clarity and whether the reveal lands as a payoff rather than a reset.

items.area: The lead casting lift is unusually narrow.
items.detail: The central role has to carry teen comedy, body-horror panic, and multiple identity performances across different bodies. That makes the project more dependent on a very specific actor than the budget footprint might suggest.

items.area: The third act turns on a lot of moving parts.
items.detail: The lab climax stacks body swaps, fire, foam, gunplay, restraints, and multiple reversals in a short span. It’s exciting on the page, but it’s also the section most likely to feel over-assembled if any one beat doesn’t land cleanly.

items.area: The branded world is more specific than it needs to be.
items.detail: TikTok, Trader Joe’s, iPhone, Ford, Honda, Mercedes, Beretta, Purina, CNN, and the New York Times all appear in a script that otherwise wants to feel timeless. None of that is fatal, but it creates clearance and substitution work that a buyer will notice.

items.area: The conspiracy logic is dense by design.
items.detail: The script has a lot of moving institutional pieces—company security, the lab, the patients, the billionaire, the medication, the foam, the disinformation campaign. That density gives the world texture, but it also means the movie is asking the audience to track a lot while the characters are changing bodies.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest strength is also its biggest pressure point: the identity twist is bold, but it asks for very clean execution to avoid confusion. Beyond that, the project is commercially attractive, but the casting lift, branded specificity, and dense conspiracy mechanics are the main conversations before a greenlight.
